paragraphs: “We proceeded to search him. The search angered him, but it also encouraged him: the whole three thousand had not been found on him, only half of it. And no doubt it was only in that moment of angry silence that the fiction of the little bag first occurred to him. No doubt he was aware himself of how improbable the story was, and he struggled painfully to make it sound more likely, to weave it into a romance that would seem plausible. In such cases the first duty, the chief task of the investigators, is to keep the criminal from preparing himself, to pounce on him unexpectedly so that he blurts out his cherished ideas in all their simplicity, improbability and inconsistency. The criminal can be made to speak only by the sudden and seemingly casual mention of some new fact, some circumstance of great importance to the case, of which he had no previous idea and could not have foreseen. We had such a fact ready. It was Grigory’s evidence about the open door through which the prisoner had run out. He had completely forgotten that door and had not even suspected that Grigory could have seen it.

“The effect was amazing. He leapt up and shouted at us, ‘Then Smerdyakov murdered him, it was Smerdyakov!’ In doing so he betrayed the basis of the defense he was holding back, and betrayed it in its most improbable form, for Smerdyakov could only have committed the murder after the prisoner had knocked Grigory down and run away. When we told him that Grigory had seen the door open before he fell, and had heard Smerdyakov behind the screen as he came out of his bedroom, Karamazov was positively crushed. My esteemed and witty colleague, Nikolay Parfenovitch, told me afterwards that he was almost moved to tears at the sight of him. And to improve his position, the prisoner hurried to tell us about the much-talked-of little bag. So be it, you shall hear this romance!

“Gentlemen of the jury, I have told you already why I consider this romance not only an absurdity, but the most improbable invention that could have been put forward in the circumstances. If one tried, for a bet, to invent the most unlikely story, one could hardly find anything more incredible. The trouble with such stories is that the triumphant romancers can always be thrown into confusion and crushed by the very details in which real life is so rich, and which these unhappy, involuntary storytellers neglect as insignificant trifles. Oh, they have no thought to spare for such details. Their minds are fixed on their grand invention as a whole. And imagine anyone daring to stop them over a trifle! But that is how they are caught. The prisoner was asked, ‘Where did you get the stuff for your little bag, and who made it for you?’ ‘I made it myself.’ ‘And where did you get the linen?’ The prisoner was positively offended. He thought it almost insulting to be asked such a trivial question, and would you believe it, his resentment was genuine! But they are all like that. ‘I tore it off my shirt.’ ‘Then tomorrow we shall find that shirt among your linen, with a piece torn off.’ And only think, gentlemen of the jury, if we really had found that torn shirt (and how could we have failed to find it in his chest of drawers or trunk?), that would have been a fact, a material fact in support of his statement! But he was incapable of that reflection. ‘I don’t remember, it may not have been off my shirt, I sewed it up in one of my landlady’s caps.’ ‘What sort of cap?’ ‘It was an old cotton rag of hers lying about.’ ‘And do you remember that clearly?’ ‘No, I don’t.’ And he was angry, very angry, and yet imagine not remembering it! At the most terrible moments of a man’s life, for instance when he is being led to execution, he remembers just such trifles. He will forget everything except some green roof that flashed past him on the road, or a jackdaw on a cross. That he will remember. This man hid the making of that little bag from his household. He must have remembered his humiliating fear that someone might come in and find him with a needle in his hand, and how at the slightest sound he slipped behind the screen (there is a screen in his lodgings).

“But, gentlemen of the jury, why do I tell you all this, all these details, these trifles?” cried Ippolit Kirillovitch suddenly. “Just because the prisoner persists in these absurdities to this very moment. He has explained nothing since that fatal night two months ago. He has not added one real, illuminating fact to his earlier fantastic statements; all of it is trivialities. ‘You must believe it on my honor.’ Oh, we are glad to believe it, we are eager to believe it, even if only on his word of honor! Are we jackals thirsting for human blood? Show us a single fact in the prisoner’s favor and we shall rejoice. But let it be a substantial, real fact, and not a conclusion drawn from the prisoner’s expression by his own brother, or the idea that when he beat himself on the breast he must have meant to point to the little bag, in the darkness, too. We shall rejoice at the new fact. We shall be the first to withdraw our charge, and we shall hasten to withdraw it. But now justice cries out, and we persist. We cannot withdraw anything.”

Ippolit Kirillovitch went on to his final peroration. He looked as if he were in a fever. He spoke of the blood that cried out for vengeance, the blood of a father murdered by his son for the base motive of robbery! He pointed to the tragic and glaring consistency of the facts.

“And whatever you may hear from the talented and celebrated counsel for the defense,” Ippolit Kirillovitch could not resist adding, “whatever eloquent and touching appeals may be made to your feelings, remember that at this moment you are in a temple of justice. Remember that you are the champions of our justice, the champions of our holy Russia, of her principles, her family, everything she holds sacred! Yes, you represent Russia here at this moment, and your verdict will be heard not in this hall only but will echo throughout the whole of Russia. All Russia will hear you, as her champions and her judges, and she will be encouraged or disheartened by your verdict. Do not disappoint Russia and her expectations. Our fatal troika dashes on in headlong flight, perhaps to destruction, and for a long time now all over Russia men have stretched out imploring hands and called a halt to its furious, reckless course. And if other nations stand aside from that troika, it may be not from respect, as the poet would like to believe, but simply from horror. From horror, perhaps from disgust. And it is well that they stand aside, but perhaps one day they will cease to do so. They will form a firm wall confronting the hurrying apparition and will check the frenzied rush of our lawlessness, for the sake of their own safety, enlightenment and civilization. Already we have heard voices of alarm from Europe; they are beginning to sound. Do not tempt them! Do not add to their growing hatred by a sentence justifying the murder of a father by his son!”

Though Ippolit Kirillovitch was genuinely moved, he ended his speech with this rhetorical appeal, and the effect was extraordinary. When he had finished, he went out hurriedly and, as I have mentioned before, almost fainted in the next room. There was no applause in the court, but serious people were pleased. The ladies were less satisfied, though even they were pleased with his eloquence, especially as they had no fears about the outcome of the trial and had full trust in Fetyukovitch. “He will speak at last and of course carry everything before him.”

Everyone looked at Mitya. He had sat silent through the whole of the prosecutor’s speech, with clenched teeth, hands clasped and head bowed. Only from time to time he raised his head and listened, especially when Grushenka was spoken of. When the prosecutor mentioned Rakitin’s opinion of her, a smile of contempt and anger crossed his face, and he murmured, rather audibly, “The Bernards!” When Ippolit Kirillovitch described how he had questioned and tortured him at Mokroe, Mitya raised his head and listened with intense curiosity. At one point he seemed about to jump up and cry out, but he controlled himself and only shrugged his shoulders scornfully. Afterwards people talked about the end of the speech and about the prosecutor’s feat in examining the prisoner at Mokroe, and jeered at Ippolit Kirillovitch. “The man could not resist boasting of his cleverness,” they said.
The court adjourned, but only for a short interval, a quarter of an hour or twenty minutes at most. There was a hum of conversation and exclamations in the audience. I remember some of them.
“A weighty speech,” a gentleman in one group remarked gravely.
“He brought in too much psychology,” said another voice.
“But it was all true, the absolute truth!”
“Yes, he’s first-rate at it.”
“He summed it all up.”
“Yes, he summed us up, too,” chimed in another voice. “Do you remember how at the beginning of his speech he made out we were all like Fyodor Pavlovitch?”
“And at the end, too. But that was all rot.”
“And obscure, too.”
“He got a little too carried away.”
“It’s unjust, it’s unjust.”
“No, it was smartly done, anyway. He’s had a long wait, but he’s had his say, ha ha!”
“What will the counsel for the defense say?”
In another group I heard:
“He had no business taking a jab at the Petersburg man like that. ‘Appealing to your feelings’—do you remember?”
“Yes, that was clumsy of him.”
“He was in too much of a hurry.”
“He’s a nervous man.”
“We laugh, but what must the prisoner be feeling?”
“Yes, what must it be like for Mitya?”
In a third group:
“Who is that lady, the fat one with the lorgnette, sitting at the end?”
“She’s a general’s wife, divorced. I know her.”
“That’s why she has the lorgnette.”
“She’s not good for much.”
“Oh, no, she’s a piquante little woman.”
“Two places beyond her there’s a little fair woman. She’s prettier.”
“They caught him smartly at Mokroe, didn’t they, eh?”
“Oh, smart enough. We’ve heard it before. How often he has told the story in people’s houses!”
“And he couldn’t resist doing it now. That’s vanity.”
“He’s a man with a grievance, he he!”
“Yes, and quick to take offense. And there was too much rhetoric, such long sentences.”
“Yes, he tries to frighten us, he kept trying to frighten us. Do you remember about the troika? Something like ‘They have Hamlets, but so far we have only Karamazovs!’ That was cleverly said!”
“That was to appease the liberals. He’s afraid of them.”
“Yes, and he’s afraid of the lawyer, too.”
“Yes, what will Fetyukovitch say?”
“Whatever he says, he won’t get around our peasants.”
“Don’t you think so?”
A fourth group:
“What he said about the troika was good, that part about the other nations.”
“And what he said was true, that other nations won’t put up with it.”
“What do you mean?”

“Why, last week in the English Parliament a Member got up and, speaking about the Nihilists, asked the Ministry whether it wasn’t high time to intervene and educate this barbarous people. Ippolit was thinking of him, I know he was. He was talking about it last week.”
“Not an easy job.”
“Not an easy job? Why not?”
“Why, we’d shut up Kronstadt and not let them have any corn. Where would they get it?”
“In America. They get it from America now.”
“Nonsense!”
But the bell rang, and everyone rushed back to their places. Fetyukovitch mounted the tribune.
